passage:
In the government school at Nandgaon, Madam asked Tanuja to read the Hindi lesson aloud. Tanuja stood up, and the words on the page seemed to jump. "The farmer... the far... the fra..." Someone giggled. Tanuja crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and said in a deep voice, "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!" The whole class burst out laughing, and so did she. Madam smiled but didn't move on to the next reader.
After the bell, Madam called her over. "You made them laugh very well. Was the reading hard today?" Tanuja shrugged and pulled another face. Her friend Zeenat, waiting by the door, noticed Tanuja's fingers twisting the end of her plait.

qa.q: What did Tanuja say in a deep voice?
qa.a: "The farmer has lost his reading glasses!"

qa.q: Why did Tanuja pull a funny face instead of trying the word again?
qa.a: She was embarrassed as the words jumped and someone giggled; the joke let her take charge so the class laughed with her, not at her.

qa.q: What choice did Madam make after the bell, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She praised the joke but gently asked if the reading was hard, which looks past the clowning to the worry underneath.

qa.q: What might Zeenat have understood from Tanuja's twisting fingers?
qa.a: Zeenat may have sensed that Tanuja was more worried than her funny faces showed.

grounding: A girl who stumbles while reading aloud turns it into a joke so the class laughs with her, while small signs show her worry.

passage:
In Year 5 at a primary school in Leeds, Bilal was halfway through his book report when he said "volcano" as "vol-CAN-o". Marek sniggered. Bilal froze for a second. Then he threw his arms up, wobbled like an erupting mountain and shouted, "KA-BOOM! Vol-CAN-o has exploded!" Everyone laughed, even Mrs Hughes. Bilal grinned and finished the report in a silly voice.
At lunch he did it again for the table, and again in the queue for the bus. At home, though, he asked his mum to listen to him read the report five times, until he could say every word right.

qa.q: Which word did Bilal say wrongly?
qa.a: "Volcano", as "vol-CAN-o".

qa.q: What does Bilal reading the report five times at home suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was worried and embarrassed about the mistake, even though his joke made it look as if he didn't care.

qa.q: What could Mrs Hughes try the next time Bilal reads aloud?
qa.a: Enjoy his humour, but offer a quiet practice run beforehand, so he doesn't need a joke to escape the worry. 🙂

qa.q: How might Marek feel after the snigger turned into the whole class laughing with Bilal?
qa.a: Marek may have felt the moment slip away, since the joke turned the laughter from mocking into sharing.

grounding: A boy in England turns a reading slip into a clowning act that gets the class laughing with him, but practises anxiously at home.

passage:
During the Class 6 spelling bee in the school hall, Alka misspelled "necessary" in front of two hundred students. She paused, then pretended to faint across the stage. The hall roared. Even the principal laughed.
For the rest of the week Alka joked through everything. She wore her tie as a headband in maths, answered science questions in a robot voice, and pulled faces whenever a teacher looked her way. Her class teacher, Jasleen Ma'am, noticed she hadn't handed in homework since the bee. On Friday she kept Alka back for a minute. "You're the funniest person in this class," she said. "And I think you might also be worried about something. Want to tell me?"
Alka stopped smiling. "I always get spellings wrong," she said quietly.

qa.q: Which word did Alka misspell at the spelling bee?
qa.a: "Necessary".

qa.q: Why might Alka have joked through everything for the rest of the week?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and worried about her spelling, and constant clowning kept everyone laughing so nobody saw the worry.

qa.q: What choice did Jasleen Ma'am make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She praised Alka's humour and then gently named that she might be worried, which made it safe for Alka to admit the real problem.

qa.q: How might the students in the hall have seen Alka's faint?
qa.a: As a hilarious bit of fun, probably without guessing she was embarrassed underneath.

grounding: After a spelling-bee mistake a girl clowns constantly, and a teacher notices the joking hides a worry.

passage:
I'm Gurpreet, and I sit behind Madhuri in Class 4. On Monday Miss asked her to read the recipe in our English book. At "ingredients" she said "in-GREE-dee-ents" and a couple of kids snickered. Madhuri stopped, put on a posh voice like a TV cook, waved her ruler like a spoon and said, "Today, darlings, we cook the in-GREE-dee-ents!" The whole class cracked up. Even Miss smiled.
She's always funny. But she does it every single time it's her turn to read. On reading days she chews her pencil flat and asks to go to the washroom before English. Maybe she just likes making us laugh. Or maybe she'd rather we laugh at the joke than at her.

qa.q: Which word did Madhuri stumble on?
qa.a: "Ingredients"; she said "in-GREE-dee-ents".

qa.q: Why might Madhuri turn the mistake into a TV-cook act?
qa.a: The joke lets her take control of the moment so the class laughs with her, not at her, hiding embarrassment and maybe worry about reading.

qa.q: How could Miss support Madhuri after noticing the pattern?
qa.a: Miss could quietly check whether reading aloud is hard for Madhuri and offer practice or a heads-up before her turn, while still enjoying her humour.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see the jokes differently from the rest of the class?
qa.a: Gurpreet enjoys them too, but notices the chewed pencil and washroom trips on reading days, so the jokes look like they might be covering worry.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a child who stumbles while reading and turns it into a silly act that gets the class laughing with her, with signs of hidden worry.

passage:
Monday. In science, Hafsa, ten, read "photosynthesis" as "photo-sin-thesis". Someone giggled. She held up an invisible camera and said, "Say cheese, everyone, it's photo-sin time!" The class roared, and her ears stopped burning.
Wednesday. It was her turn again. Before she even started, she crossed her eyes and made a fish face. Everyone laughed, waiting for more. "Hafsa, just read, please," said the teacher. That evening she shoved her reading book under the bed. "I'm the funny one, Noor baji," she told her cousin. "Not the reading one."
Saturday. Noor baji sat with her on the floor. They clapped out hard words together: pho-to-syn-the-sis. Hafsa still made jokes, silly ones about plants eating sunshine. But she read the whole next page, stopping only twice.

qa.q: How did Hafsa read "photosynthesis" on Monday?
qa.a: As "photo-sin-thesis".

qa.q: What does "I'm the funny one, not the reading one" reveal about Hafsa's worry?
qa.a: It reveals she worries she is bad at reading, and being funny feels like a safer thing to be known for.

qa.q: What choice by Noor baji on Saturday helped?
qa.a: Practising hard words with Hafsa by clapping out the syllables, without taking her jokes away, so reading felt less scary 🙂

qa.q: What might the teacher be thinking when saying, "Hafsa, just read, please"?
qa.a: The teacher may think Hafsa is just being silly on purpose, without seeing the worry about reading underneath the fish face.

grounding: Illustrates a child who covers reading stumbles with jokes that make the class laugh with her, while the clowning hides a worry that shows at home.
